content: The Australian census is conducted every five years by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS). The most recent census was held on August 8, 2006. Before the introduction of regular censuses in 1961, censuses were conducted in 1901, 1911, 1921, 1933, 1947, and 1954. Participation in the census is mandatory for all households, except for questions regarding religion and the archiving of personal census details. The census counts all individuals present in Australia and its territories on census night, excluding foreign diplomats and their families. The Census and Statistics Act of 1905 led to the establishment of the Commonwealth Bureau of Census and Statistics (CBCS) in 1906, which was renamed the Australian Bureau of Statistics in 1975. Census data is collected and published based on geographic areas defined by the Australian Standard Geographical Classification (ASGC). The smallest spatial unit for census data collection is the Census Collection District (CD), which can be aggregated to cover larger areas such as Statistical Local Areas (SLAs). The ASGC hierarchy includes Collection Districts, Statistical Local Areas, Statistical Subdivisions, Statistical Divisions, States or Territories, and Australia as a whole. The Census and Statistics Act of 1905 and the Privacy Act of 1988 ensure that no personally identifiable information is released to other government organizations or the public. However, the 2001 census introduced an option for individuals to allow their personal data to be archived by the National Archives of Australia and made publicly available after 99 years. In 2001, 54% of Australians agreed to this. Confidentialized census data is also made available to researchers under strict legal commitments. In 1967, a referendum approved amendments to the Australian Constitution regarding Indigenous Australians. One amendment removed Section 127, which had excluded Aboriginal natives from being counted in population calculations for parliamentary seat allocation and Commonwealth grants. Aboriginal people living in settled areas were counted in censuses before 1967, but the section aimed to prevent states like Queensland and Western Australia from gaining additional seats or funds due to their large Aboriginal populations. Ancestry data was first included in the 1986 census, but inconsistent responses led to its exclusion in 1991 and 1996. By 2001, it was reintroduced to inform government policies, focusing on individuals born overseas or with parents born overseas. Respondents could report multiple ancestries, but only the first two were coded. The data was classified using the Australian Standard Classification of Cultural and Ethnic Groups (ASCCEG), which is tailored to Australian needs and based on geographic origin and cultural characteristics. Australia's first census was conducted in November 1828 in the colony of New South Wales. Earlier population counts were based on musters, where inhabitants were gathered for counting. The 1828 census recorded a white population of 36,598, of whom 20,870 were free and 15,728 were convicts. Indigenous Australians were not counted. By 1881, a simultaneous census was conducted across the colonies as part of a British Empire-wide effort, though questions varied between colonies, complicating data analysis. The first national census was conducted in April 1911, following the establishment of the Commonwealth Bureau of Census and Statistics. Data tabulation was done manually, with over 4 million cards sorted and counted. The census revealed a population of 4,455,005. Subsequent censuses introduced technological advancements, such as automatic machine tabulation in 1921, which used punched cards and electric sorting machines. The 2006 census, conducted on August 8, counted 19,855,288 people in Australia, including 455,031 Indigenous Australians and 206,358 overseas visitors. The census included 60 questions, with all but those on religion and data retention being mandatory. It cost approximately AUD $300 million to conduct. For the first time, respondents could complete the census online via the eCensus. By August 17, over 720,000 households had submitted their census online, representing 4% of estimated dwellings. IBM assisted the ABS with the eCensus infrastructure, which remained fully operational throughout the census period.
